::: {#exr-miller-deriv-classify-critical-points}
#### Classifying critical points with the second derivative test

Adapted from @problifesavercalc, Question 1.1.11.

An [optimization algorithm](optimization.qmd#def-optimization-algorithm) such as
[Newton's method](optimization.qmd#def-newton-method)
or [gradient descent](optimization.qmd#def-gradient-descent)
can stop at a [critical point](#def-critical-point),
which may be a local [maximum](algebra.qmd#def-maximum), a local [minimum](algebra.qmd#def-minimum), or neither.
The [second derivative test](#thm-second-derivative-test) tells these apart.

Consider the [cubic](algebra.qmd#def-cubic-polynomial)

$$f(x) = 4x^3 - 3x^2.$$

Find its critical points,
and decide whether each is a local maximum, a local minimum, or an [inflection point](#def-inflection-point).
:::

::: {#sol-miller-deriv-classify-critical-points}
Compute the first derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)
&= 12x^2 - 6x \\
&= 6x(2x - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $f'(x) = 0$ gives critical points at $x = 0$ and $x = 1/2$.

Compute the second derivative:

$$f''(x) = 24x - 6$$

Apply the second derivative test at each critical point:

- At $x = 0$: $f''(0) = -6 < 0$, so $x = 0$ is a strict local maximum.
- At $x = 1/2$:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  f''(1/2) &= 24(1/2) - 6 \\
  &= 6 \\
  &> 0,
  \end{aligned}
  $$

  so $x = 1/2$ is a strict local minimum.

Inflection points occur where the second derivative changes sign ($f''(x) = 0$ at $x = 1/4$). Because $f''$ is non-zero at both critical points, neither is an inflection point.
:::
